newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: U.S. breaks world trade rules with boycott - Cuba.
newsitem.headline: U.S. breaks world trade rules with boycott - Cuba.

text.p: Cuba used the first Ministerial Conference of the World Trade Organisation on Monday to accuse the United States of grossly violating the body's rules with its 35-year economic blockade of the island.

Havana's external trade minister Ricardo Cabrisas Ruiz told the gathering that the blockade and the recent Helms-Burton law aimed at foreign investors were part of an "economic war" against the communist-ruled Caribbean power.

"Cuba is a socialist state which has carried out deep transformations in its economy and continues to do so to adjust to the world in which we live without in any way renouncing its political position," he declared.

Measures taken over the past three years, during which there has been a limited liberalisation of the once strictly state-controlled economy, had enabled the country to increase both imports and exports and spark new growth.

This had been achieved, he said, "in spite of the fact that the country is still subjected to a criminal and illegal economic, financial and trade blockade which is in flagrant violation of the rules of this organisation."
"The most powerful nation in the world has imposed an economic war on us," the Cuban minister declared.

Cuba was a founder member in 1948 of the WTO's predecessor, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, and remained in the old body -- seen then by other communist states as a "capitalist club" -- after the 1959 revolution.

U.S. policy towards the island has become a major issue in the 128-member WTO and other international bodies including the Organisation of American States over the past few months following passage of the Helms-Burton bill.

The measure, named after its Congressional sponsors who have sworn to bring about the ouster of President Fidel Castro, was signed by President Bill Clinton after the downing by Cuban jets of two planes flown by anti-Castro exiles near Havana.

The law allows Cubans and U.S. citizens who fled after the communist revolution in 1959 to take action in U.S. courts against foreign companies who "traffic" -- or invest -- in nationalised property they once owned on the island.

Also allowing for the refusal of U.S. visas to executives of these companies and their families, it has caused a major row with the European Union which has taken Washington to the WTO Dispute Settlement Body (DSB) over the issue.

The DSB has set up a panel to determine whether the law does run against WTO open trade rules. The United States has signalled it will argue it is allowed under a special regulation to waive these in defence of national sovereignty.

Cabrisas Ruiz told the WTO ministers, including U.S. Acting Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky, that the blockade and Helms-Burton had been imposed "because our people has committed the crime of wanting to maintain its independence, its sovereignty, its self- determination and its national dignity." But Havana would keep its own pledges on open trade to the two-year-old WTO "and will continue as ever to cooperate to ensure its success," he added.
